evidence: 4 of 6 statements are neutral and value the student's own voice rather than banning AI: University of Denver 'they should be encouraged to have their own voices come through in their written work'; Smith College 'It is the student's voice we want to hear, not the voice of generative AI'; UPR Rio Piedras 'la originalidad y el esfuerzo personal son esenciales para la evaluación del aprendizaje'. Only Montana State ('Only content done by a student ... is accepted') is a prohibition.

The deciding statements are about what counts when work is evaluated: UPR Rio Piedras 'esenciales para la evaluación del aprendizaje'; Montana State 'Only content done by a student or as part of an assigned group is accepted'; the directive itself says 'what counts for assessment'. (Georgia Tech's design question is the only clear before-course one.)

current: Instructors should grade only the work students did themselves, not AI output.
proposed: Instructors should assign writing in writing-intensive courses to be done without AI.
evidence: Both statements are about assigning AI-free writing, not grading: Bucknell 'all W courses will emphasize and assign writing to be completed without genAI use'; 'genAI use not be permitted at all in students' writing processes in W1s.'

Being wary of vendor claims takes no position on AI use: University of North Dakota 'Be wary of claims by third-party vendors.'; UT Health Science Center 'be cautious of claims by product providers'; Michigan State 'should never be assumed to be safe, secure, or private'.

The instructor decides whether AI is allowed: Stony Brook 'AI may be used in graduate classes if and only if the instructor permits it'; Southern Mississippi 'faculty must approve its use for coursework, supervised research, and examinations'.

A procedural duty that holds whatever the course stance on AI: Stony Brook 'prior permission for an individual policy must be received in writing from the UPD'; 'with prior written approval of the Undergraduate Program Director (UPD)'.

Telling students the rules; 8 of 10 shown statements are neutral: University of Iowa 'include specific language about academic misconduct'; University of Delaware 'consider if they should include an explicit reminder about plagiarism and academic [integrity]'; University of Idaho 'citing the Student Code of Conduct E-1.c would be useful'.

The instructor decides whether uploading is allowed: UC Santa Cruz 'whether you will allow them to upload your course materials into a generative AI tool'; University of Pennsylvania 'you may wish to set a policy that prohibits sharing your materials with AI tools'; Nova Southeastern 'you may consider allowing course content'.

current: Your students may opt out of AI-assisted grading and request human review.
proposed: Let your students opt out of AI-assisted grading and request human review of their work.
evidence: Statements put the duty on the instructor, which the current wording omits: University of Nebraska Omaha 'Instructors should offer a human-alternative (e.g., teacher, TA) for those who do not consent.'; University of Utah 'Students must be able to opt out of AI-assisted grading without penalty.'

Mostly neutral general ethics duties; the 3 restrict statements all come from one university (Oregon State): Davidson 'subject to professional standards and guidelines issued by the Vice President for Academic Affairs'; University of South Florida 'Faculty should also consider the ethical use of generative AI in their own teaching practices'; NDSU 'have a responsibility for their own use of'.

current: Get student permission before putting student work into AI tools.
proposed: Tell students when you use AI on their work, and get their permission before putting their work into AI tools.
evidence: Several statements ask for disclosure, not permission: Appalachian State 'Disclose any intended use of AI in the assessment of student work'; University of Maine 'Instructors should inform students if they use an AI tool to assess students' work'; alongside permission: University of Nebraska Omaha 'have explicit approval from students'.

Every statement is about grading: Georgia State 'treats grading and assessment of student work as automated decision-making, which requires extreme caution'; Northeastern 'any use of generative AI to grade open-ended student responses'; Penn State 'Any use of software to assist with grading must comply with Senate Policy 47-20'.

current: Keep feedback and faculty-student engagement human-centered and personal rather than AI-generated.
proposed: Keep feedback and faculty-student engagement human-centered and personal, including when you use AI.
evidence: Statements ask for a human-centered approach, not for no AI: James Madison 'Faculty are encouraged to uphold a human-centered approach to feedback.'; Wake Forest 'commitment to meaningful and person-centered faculty-student engagement should guide these applications of GAI technology'.

Watching student process is a duty that holds whatever the stance on AI use: James Madison 'Lean on process instead: drafts, checkpoints, short reflections, and conversations.'; UNC Charlotte 'alternatives, such as (i) requiring a short reflection paper'.

Statements are about choosing the exam format (design): Boise State 'Change all exams to be in-class.'; Cornell 'If GenAI can solve your take-home exam question, rework the question, or move to in-person'; Cornell 'moving assessments from take-home to in-class'. The brief says designing an exam format is before-course.

Responding to misuse holds whatever the course stance on AI; 4 of 6 statements are neutral: Montana 'Unintentional use + policy unclear = Education + no penalty or resubmission option'; Oklahoma State 'consequences of AI misuse, such as failing the assignment or course'; Portland State 'Give a proper grade for the assignment or exam in question.'

current: Apply proportionate responses to AI misuse, taking account of intent, policy clarity and prior offenses.
proposed: Respond to AI misuse with consequences that fit the case, from education or resubmission to failing the assignment, taking account of intent and how clear the policy was.
evidence: No statement mentions prior offenses (all 6 shown): Montana 'Unintentional use + policy clear = Warning + resubmission or partial credit'; Oklahoma State 'consequences of AI misuse, such as failing the assignment or course'; University of North Florida 'Apply existing sanctions, including forfeiture of academic credit'.

current: Instructors should respond to AI misuse in proportion, weighing intent, rule clarity and past offenses.
proposed: Instructors should respond to AI misuse in proportion, weighing intent and how clear the rules were.
evidence: 'past offenses' appears in none of the 6 statements; Montana's rules turn on intent and clarity: 'Unintentional use + policy unclear' / 'Unintentional use + policy clear'.

current: Instructors should not ban AI, restricting it only when the assignment tests that very skill.
proposed: Instructors should keep AI-assisted work focused on students' own interpretation and critical analysis.
evidence: The only statement is about what student work should focus on, not about banning: Azusa Pacific 'make sure the focus is on their interpretation and critical analysis of the results'.

current: You may define in course policies which AI data analysis uses are permitted.
proposed: You may allow students to use AI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data.
evidence: The only statement lists an allowed use; it says nothing about defining which uses: University of Louisiana at Lafayette 'Use of GAI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data'.

All 7 statements are 'may': Yeshiva 'AI tools may assist with generating draft feedback or flagging patterns'; Cornell 'GAI may have selective utility in assisting in providing feedback for low-stakes formative assessment'; Wisconsin-Madison 'AI can assist with generating ideas for praise'.

current: You may use AI to help draft formative feedback, flag patterns and generate ideas, provided you personalize the feedback.
proposed: You may use AI to help draft formative feedback, flag patterns in student responses and generate ideas for feedback.
evidence: None of the 7 statements mentions personalizing feedback: Yeshiva 'AI tools may assist with generating draft feedback or flagging patterns'; South Dakota 'Identifying patterns in student responses'; Georgia State 'AI-generated formative feedback can be an important part of a scaffolded assignment'.

current: Instructors should personalize any feedback they draft with AI before giving it to students.
proposed: Instructors may use AI to help draft feedback and spot patterns in student work.
evidence: No statement asks for personalization; all permit AI help: Yeshiva 'AI tools may assist with generating draft feedback or flagging patterns'; UMass Boston 'evaluate student work and generate feedback on assignments, essays, and other projects'.

Attending training does not invite or promote AI use itself; many statements are neutral: Cornell 'Take advantage of one of the workshops offered by CTI'; Gonzaga 'Check the CTA Events schedule regularly for AI related training and workshops for faculty.'; Alaska Fairbanks 'Join us for upcoming workshops to explore and share ideas.'

Statements set how AI should be used, not that it should be used; two are neutral and the two 'encourage' ones are one Texas Tech sentence repeated: Florida State 'AI tools should be used in ways that support student learning outcomes and promote transparency'; UTSA 'strike a balance that upholds academic integrity while harnessing the benefits of technology'; Texas Tech 'should prioritize human agency'.

current: Use AI to support learning outcomes and balance academic integrity with its benefits, prioritizing human agency.
proposed: When you use AI, use it in ways that support student learning outcomes and transparency, balance academic integrity with its benefits, and prioritize human agency.
evidence: The statements condition use rather than ask instructors to use AI: Florida State 'AI tools should be used in ways that support student learning outcomes and promote transparency'.

current: Instructors should assign tasks where students use or critique AI after doing their own work first.

current: Instructors should assign tasks where students use or critique AI after doing their own work first.

evidence: The statement sets no 'after their own work first' condition: Colorado School of Mines 'Invite students to use custom AI chatbots (Google Gems)'.

proposed: You may use AI to identify errors in student code and suggest possible fixes.

current: Teach responsible AI use rather than banning or policing it.

evidence: No statement mentions banning; they contrast teaching with policing: University of South Carolina 'Rather than police and penalize AI use'; University of Kansas 'Instructor time is far better spent on helping students use AI responsibly than on trying'; UTEP 'The goal is not to catch AI misuse but rather to cultivate responsible'.

current: Instructors should teach responsible AI use rather than banning or policing it.
proposed: Instructors should teach responsible AI use rather than policing it.
evidence: 'banning' appears in none of the 4 statements: University of South Carolina 'Rather than police and penalize AI use'; UTEP 'The goal is not to catch AI misuse'.

Sharing materials with colleagues takes no position on AI use; 2 of 3 statements are neutral: Prairie View A&M 'faculty are invited to share their AI-related syllabus statements'; Smith College 'please consider sharing your assignments with colleagues'.

Assessing impact and adjusting is a duty that holds whatever the stance; 3 of 4 statements are neutral: VCU 'Regularly assess the impact of using AI in your course and student learning outcomes'; VCU 'Solicit feedback on course activities that use AI, and adjust when needed'; UTSA 'also measure the development of foundational skills'.

All 10 shown statements are neutral duties to align with local policy (the parallel P77.01 is already 'none'): Duquesne 'Course AI policies should be consistent with any existing school and departmental policies'; University of Alabama 'Instructors should follow departmental and college guidelines as applicable'.

All 4 statements are 'may' and the directive is two 'may' clauses: University of Alabama 'variation from a department-wide policy is permissible, but should be documented'; East Tennessee State 'The department or instructor of record may also establish policies'; Jackson State 'individual faculty ... may have additional criteria in their syllabus'.

Telling students the rules (the brief's own example of 'none'); shown statements are neutral: Alaska Fairbanks 'Instructors should be clear with students on what, if any, and how Generative AI'; University of Alabama 'Whether AI use is permitted, restricted or prohibited overall'; Abilene Christian 'define what is acceptable and not acceptable in your class'.

Stating rules per assignment is a communication duty; all 10 shown statements are neutral: Augusta 'Clearly define what level of AI assistance is permitted for each specific assignment'; American University 'Give guidance for every assignment'; Carleton 'you'll also need to write clear AI policies for any assignment that deviates'.

Co-creating rules needs the students, and statements place it at the start of term: UCLA 'forming a policy in collaboration with your students at the beginning of the quarter'; UC Santa Barbara 'making some common ground rules with students about what is and isn't acceptable'.

current: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy together with their students.
proposed: Instructors should disclose to students whether and how they use generative AI.

The proposed label is the existing P47.01 theme label.

current: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy together with their students.
proposed: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
evidence: No statement mentions writing the policy with students; they ask for a definition in the policy: Austin Community College 'Definition of GAI – Define what GAI is in the context of the course'; East Tennessee State University 'Your policy should clearly outline what does (not) count as GenAI'.

current: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy together with their students.
proposed: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
evidence: Statements are about the tone and wording the instructor uses, not co-writing with students: Carleton College 'the best syllabus statements are clear, concise, and explanatory rather than punitive'; University of California, Santa Cruz 'Use welcoming and inclusive language'.

current: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy together with their students.
proposed: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
evidence: Both statements only ask for a syllabus notice, nothing about students co-writing it: Abilene Christian University and California State University, Fullerton 'A notice about using AI ethically and responsibly'.

current: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy together with their students.

evidence: Neither statement involves students in writing the policy: Florida State University 'Ethical use should be a primary consideration when making decisions about implementing AI'; University of Nebraska Omaha 'Ensure AI integration in your class promotes ethical and responsible use of AI.'

current: Instructors should redesign assignments and grading so AI cannot easily do the work for students.

evidence: Statements are about documentation requirements, not making assignments AI-resistant: Mercer University 'What drafts, notes, sources, prompts, outputs, or other process records should students retain?'; University of Wisconsin-Madison 'whether to require students to turn in, or at least retain, AI chat transcripts'; Georgia Institute of Technology 'do you want them to show their prompts and/or the GenAI output'.

current: Instructors should redesign assignments and grading so AI cannot easily do the work for students.
proposed: Instructors should state in the rubric whether and how AI use counts in grading.
evidence: Several statements make AI use a graded element, the opposite of keeping AI from doing the work: Azusa Pacific University 'The grading rubric will include an element of the effective use of A.I.'; Austin Community College 'In courses that permit or require GAI, clarify if and how its use' and 'The use of GAI will be part of the grading rubric'; Clark Atlanta University 'Grading criteria for AI-assisted work'.

current: Instructors should set penalties for AI misuse before the course, favoring teaching over policing.
proposed: Instructors should select or develop AI tools that preserve usage data.
evidence: The only statement is about tool choice, not penalties: University of Rochester 'Instructors should select or develop GenAI tools that preserve usage data'.

current: Instructors should tell students at the start how AI misuse is detected and punished.

evidence: Statements ask the instructor to collect a baseline sample, not to tell students about detection or penalties: University of California, Santa Cruz 'consider soliciting a short handwritten writing sample from your students at the start of the'; University of Nebraska-Lincoln 'collecting an in-person writing sample early in the semester'; University of Denver 'get to know your students' writing styles.'

current: Instructors should tell students at the start how AI misuse is detected and punished.
proposed: Instructors should remind students that they are responsible for the work they submit, including any AI content in it.
evidence: Statements are about student accountability for submitted work, with nothing on detection or punishment: University of Arizona 'Remind your students that they are responsible for the quality of the work that they submit.'; University of Florida 'they are responsible for AI-generated content they submit, present, or publish.'; University of Virginia 'Remind your students that they are ultimately responsible for the work they submit.'

Statements choose the exam format and conditions (design), not grading or what counts in grading: Texas Tech University 'Timed assignments may be helpful for short written responses or quizzes.'; The University of West Florida 'Utilizing question banks and randomized testing'; CUNY City College 'will need to revert to shorter in-class work'; University of Texas Rio Grande Valley 'Appropriate time limits can reduce opportunities to search for answers externally.'

Statements ask for reminders during the course while students work, not for revising policy or keeping up: Harvey Mudd College 'Periodically remind students about the policy'; University of Delaware 'continue to communicate your expectations throughout the semester'; CUNY City College 'Remind the students of these guidelines on a regular basis'.

The act is checking submitted work for AI content when needed (detection), not reviewing or revising policy: William & Mary 'submitted work may always be reviewed, as needed, for AI-generated content'.

Georgia Institute of Technology (CS 2340), full sentence from the syllabus text: 'at this level [AI encouraged], the instructional team reserves the right to ask for proctoring and supervising mechanisms to ensure significant learning: i.e., worklogs, videos, prompt transcripts'. The request is a learning check during coursework under the AI-encouraged level, with no mention of suspected misuse.

Every statement leaves the decision to the instructor: Texas Christian University (COSC 40503) 'for course assignments except as explicitly authorized by the instructor.'; Grinnell College (CSC 261) 'unless stated otherwise by your instructor for specific activities'; Prairie View A&M University (COMP 1336) 'should an instructor permit their students to use artificial intelligence'; San Jose State University (CS 46A) 'unless the instructor explicitly states that AI use is allowed'.

The statements give the decision to the individual instructor rather than limiting AI to listed uses: East Texas A&M University (CSCI 430/440/497) 'Individual instructors may disallow entirely the use of such software for individual assignments or for the entire course.'

The course bans GAI and allows it only as an approved exception: Austin Community College (COSC 1336) 'Exceptions to this policy will only be made under specific circumstances approved by the instructor, typically where technology is used to accommodate learning differences' (the same syllabus says 'Students are not allowed to use GAI for completing assignments'); Austin Community College (CSIS 4355) 'exceptions will be made on a case-by-case basis.'

evidence: University of Vermont (CS 2510), full sentence from the syllabus text: 'I guarantee that I will never use AI to provide feedback to you on any assessments, ever.' It names feedback on assessments, not grading.

current: Instructors should never use AI to grade.
proposed: Instructors should never use AI to give students feedback on assessments.
evidence: University of Vermont (CS 2510): 'I guarantee that I will never use AI to provide feedback to you on any assessments, ever.'

current: You may talk with the student about suspected AI misuse before any report.

'and/or' does not put the conversation before any report.

current: Instructors may talk with the student about suspected AI misuse before reporting it.

evidence: Wellesley College (CS 111): 'we may, at any point in the semester, have a conversation with you about your code, and/or file an Honor Code charge against you.'

The ban is on using AI while doing the work, not on telling rules at the start: Grinnell College CSC 213 "The use of artificial intelligence or large language models is prohibited for all work in this course."; Carnegie Mellon 15-451 "You must not make use of AI tools ... that generates code, proofs, written explanations".

The encouraged use happens while students do the work: Georgia Tech CS 1301 "We encourage use of these tools as assistants when working on exercises"; UCF COP 3503C "Your group is allowed to and encouraged to use AI for this project"; Hawaii ICS 314 "Use AI to help develop code".

AI is allowed, but only through a chat interface: UC Berkeley CS 61B "this interaction must take place exclusively through browser-based chatbots"; Cornell CS 1110 "limit such work to a chat interface and refrain from agentic tools".

current: You must interact with AI only through a chat interface.
proposed: You must not use agentic AI coding tools; where AI is allowed, use it only through a chat interface.
evidence: Princeton COS 324 bans agentic tools without a chat-only rule: "Using agentic AI (e.g., Claude Code, Cursor, etc.)"; UC Berkeley CS 61B "agentic coding tools are outright banned". Only Berkeley and Cornell add the chat-only limit.

current: You must not use generative AI on homework.
proposed: You must not use generative AI, because it would remove the learning benefit of the work.
evidence: The only statement does not mention homework: USC CSCI 103L "Because use of generative AI would remove any of that benefit, we do not allow its use."

Only Princeton COS 217 ties it to evidence of a violation.

current: You should use only course-listed packages and classes, not those AI suggests.

evidence: Neither statement mentions AI suggestions: Colby CS 343 "you should only use Python packages listed in Software"; Dartmouth COSC 10 "Use Java-provided classes or methods that we have not discussed in class."

current: Students should use at most a few lines of AI code and avoid AI-written solutions.
proposed: Students should use only the packages, classes and methods the course has listed or covered.
evidence: The statements are about which packages and classes are allowed, not about lines of AI code: Colby CS 343 "you should only use Python packages listed in Software"; Dartmouth COSC 10 "Java-provided classes or methods that we have not discussed in class".
It lists no allowed uses; it requires a statement: Colby CS 151 "You cannot receive extension points without an AI usage statement."

evidence: The freedom covers work outside graded coursework, not coursework: City College of San Francisco CS 110B "Outside of class assignments and exams, I leave it up to you"; Cornell CS 1110 "generative AI for code that you do not submit to us"; USF CS 326 "Outside a session: use AI freely, and often."

proposed: You may use AI only for the limited uses your course lists, such as learning, debugging, projects or open-format homework.

The statements grant permission: Harvey Mudd CS 105 "You may use LLMs to help explain compiler error messages or runtime errors."; Penn CIS 1100 "you are welcome to use AI to help you understand what they mean"; all ten shown are coded permit.

current: Students should find bugs themselves and use AI only to explain error messages, not fix them.

evidence: No shown statement says students must find bugs themselves, and only one forbids fixes: UW CSE 123 "Asking AI to explain an error message (but not to provide a fix)"; Michigan EECS 280 allows "Understanding compiler errors or getting suggestions for debugging a problem".

current: Students should rewrite AI code examples rather than copy them, and cite AI-written documentation.

evidence: The policy permits AI-written documentation and says nothing about rewriting code examples: Loyola Marymount CMSI 1010 "Generating short documentation strings and type hints."; UC Santa Cruz CSE 30 "AI-generated text may be used for code comments".

The use concerns graded work after the deadline, not policy review: Michigan EECS 376 "after the deadline has passed" and "whether it thinks your graded solution should earn more points on our rubric".

The use concerns understanding graded test results after the deadline, not policy review: UT Austin CS 314 "You may use generative AIs to help understand why" (tests failed, per the directive, after the deadline).

The policy promotes staff help, not AI use; most statements are neutral: USC CSCI 102L "we prefer you just get help from course staff."; Pomona CSCI 105 "use your professor and TAs as the primary resource for out-of-class help rather than AI tools"; Brown CSCI 0410 "we recommend you ask a TA."

evidence: The statements set a threshold, not a limit on citing: Loyola Marymount CMSI 1010 "cite the usage if the code you utilize is nontrivial."

current: You must not use AI to analyze data, draw conclusions or interpret simulation results in graded work.
proposed: You must not use AI to analyze data, draw conclusions from experiments or data analysis, or interpret simulation results.
evidence: Rowan University: 'Analyzing data, drawing conclusions based on experiments or data analysis'; 'Using AI to interpret, process, or analyze results from simulations'. Neither statement says 'in graded work'.

4 of 7 statements are neutral facts about authorship (University of Louisville: 'be credited as authors because they cannot be held accountable'; Virginia State University: 'tools like Grammarly, ChatGPT, or Quillbot are aids, not authors.'); the rule (MIT: 'AI should never be listed as a co-author.') is about crediting, not about whether AI may be used.

The policy asks an act (not crediting AI) done when writing up work: North Carolina State University: 'no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper'; Saint Louis University: 'authorship must reflect substantive human contributions'.

The act is the student's thesis/research work, not course design: University of Alabama, Huntsville: 'Students must discuss appropriate AI tool use with their advisor prior to using these tools'; UC Santa Barbara: 'on theses, dissertations, research articles, etc. unless specifically allowed by the instructor or supervisor'. This is a default rule for how the student's AI use is treated while doing coursework, not a start-of-course act by the student: UNC Greensboro: 'use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) will be treated analogously to assistance from another person'; Stanford: 'Absent a clear statement from a course instructor'. The parallel default rule P06.10 is coded during-work.

Default rule for using and disclosing AI while doing the work: Vanderbilt University: 'the use of such tools is permitted but must be disclosed'; 'the university permits students to use generative AI tools, but they must disclose all generative'. The parallel default rule P06.10 is coded during-work.

7 of the 10 shown statements are neutral duties that hold whatever the AI rule: Clemson University: 'The work must reflect the student's understanding.'; UC Santa Cruz: 'All submitted code must be written and fully understood by you'; Bucknell: 'strive to understand the underlying principles and logic behind the AI-generated content'.

Integrity/responsibility statements with no position on AI use: Yeshiva University: 'I have reviewed and take responsibility for the accuracy and originality of the submitted work' (neutral); UC Berkeley: 'I act with honesty, integrity, and respect for others.' (neutral). Only 1 of 3 statements is restrict.

current: Do not enter assignment or exam answers into generative AI tools.
proposed: Avoid entering assignment or exam answers into generative AI tools.
evidence: University of Nevada, Las Vegas: 'or entering assignment or exam answers is not advisable' (advice, not a prohibition).

The statements define the act of submitting undisclosed AI work, not detection or sanctions: Austin Community College: 'Submitting AI-generated content as your own without disclosure'; Auburn University: 'Undisclosed use: using AI even where allowed but not disclosing how.'; Appalachian State: 'You may not use entire sentences or paragraphs suggested by an app'. The parallel policy P19.04 is coded during-work.

Verify-output duty; 7 of 10 shown statements are neutral: Georgetown University: 'Run your code and check any output to make sure that this actually works.'; Clemson University: 'Assume generated code may be insecure or incorrect.'; UAB: 'It is your responsibility to identify errors in program logic through comprehensive, documented testing.'

Verify-output duty; 9 of 10 shown statements are neutral: University of Arkansas: 'The existence of AI-generated references should be confirmed'; Arizona State University: 'ensure any AI-generated citations are correct'; University of Alabama: 'The student is responsible for verifying all bibliographic information'.

current: Use AI to explain code syntax or specific code snippets and provide examples.
proposed: You may use AI to explain code syntax or specific code snippets and to provide examples.
evidence: Both statements are options (tag choice): Brigham Young University: 'AI can be used to help understand code syntax and provide examples.'; Rochester Institute of Technology: 'Asking it to explain a specific snippet of code (one or two functions, say)'. The directive reads as an instruction.

current: Disclosure of AI use may be optional for minor uses such as finding references, brainstorming or grammar checking.
proposed: Disclosure of AI use may be optional for minor uses such as grammar checking, brainstorming, or suggesting how to organize a paper or a title.
evidence: Princeton University: 'some AI tools are permissible for use without disclosure (e.g., grammar checkers)'; Oregon State University: 'Brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper, or suggest a paper or section title'. No statement mentions finding references.

current: You may use AI for data analysis only with oversight and under transparency policies.
proposed: You may use AI for data analysis if your use complies with transparency policies.
evidence: University of Puerto Rico, Rio Piedras: 'el uso de la IA será permitido, siempre que cumpla con las políticas de transparencia' (AI use is permitted provided it complies with transparency policies). Nothing about oversight.

current: You may use AI to summarize readings only with instructor permission.
proposed: You may use AI to summarize sources for your own understanding; some policies bar summarizing assigned readings unless the instructor permits it.
evidence: Only 2 of 6 statements make permission a condition (LSU New Orleans: 'Summarizing assigned course readings unless explicitly permitted'; UNC Chapel Hill: 'Unless I specifically allow it, do not generate responses to readings using AI.'); others allow it outright (University of South Alabama: 'Condensing information for personal study or to aid in understanding'; Jackson State: 'to summarize or synthesize sources to enhance understanding').

The act is studying and practice, outside graded assessment: Clemson University: 'Generating practice questions to study (not submitting as graded work).'; University of Washington: 'using AI on an ungraded practice exercise or exploratory code'; Embry-Riddle: 'Creating non-graded examples, scenarios or visuals to support learning.'

Advice that holds whatever the AI rule, mostly neutral: George Washington University: 'it is advisable to engage in your own independent thinking before seeking support from any'; University of South Dakota: 'Start with your own ideas'; University of Kansas: 'Try to do the assignment first'. Nothing grants permission.

Prompt-writing how-to with no position on AI use; 8 of 10 shown statements neutral: San Diego State: 'Opt for clear and explicit phrasing to improve a GenAI system's understanding of your queries'; Santa Clara: 'Provide context to questions.'; University of South Dakota: 'Ask specific questions'.

The statements advise revising prompts, not using AI; half are neutral: University of Michigan-Dearborn: 'You should expect to revise prompts to get better outputs'; UIC: 'Embrace trial and error: Continuously test and refine your prompts'; even the encourage-coded ones (Abilene Christian: 'You will need to refine your prompts in order to get good outcomes.') take no position on AI use.

A security duty, no position on AI use: UTHealth Houston: 'users must use VPN while accessing the MSBMI AIChat off-campus' (neutral); UT San Antonio: 'enable this option to add an extra layer of security'.

current: Build an AI portfolio, and instructors keep evaluating and refining their teaching over time.
proposed: Consider creating and maintaining an AI portfolio throughout your time at the university.
evidence: University of Central Florida: 'consider creating and maintaining an AI Portfolio throughout your time at UCF' (a suggestion). The instructor clause comes from The University of Montana: 'Continuously evaluate and refine your teaching methods', which is not addressed to students.

proposed: students for the UCF statement; move The University of Montana statement to an instructor policy
evidence: The University of Montana: 'Continuously evaluate and refine your teaching methods' addresses instructors (1 of 2 statements).

Swarthmore College: 'Confirm what's acceptable before using genAI tools for resumes, cover letters, and interviewing' is a student check before a use, not course design or set-up; the related career-preparation policies P119.02 and P119.03 are coded during-work.

What counts in grading: University of Alabama at Birmingham: 'AI generated submissions cannot achieve a passing grade.'; University of North Texas: 'AI generated submissions cannot achieve a passing grade'.

current: Your AI use is documented and graded, and AI use makes your work harder to evaluate.
proposed: In some courses part of your grade evaluates your documentation of AI use, and AI use can make it harder for your instructor to evaluate your work.
evidence: Only one university grades documentation: University of Alabama at Birmingham: 'A portion of your term grade will evaluate your documentation of AI use'; University of Florida: 'Use of AI would make it harder to evaluate your work.'; CU Denver: 'your faculty member is unable to evaluate your learning'. The directive states the grading as universal.
